subject: One line of awkward small talk that one robot says to another while they ride an elevator together.
gate: The written text must be UTF-8 of 1 to 200 characters, not only white space.
source_of_criteria: The judge's brief published in the competition bundle (RULES.txt 'The judge'). The five criteria are listed most important first; the weights below read that order literally and are the only place the order is turned into numbers.

criteria.brief: Reads as one funny line of awkward small talk that one robot says to another in an elevator; anything else loses to any entry on the subject.
criteria.grading: 2 = an elevator act the line is doing (going up, which floor, the doors, the ride) plus a second robot addressed, and no third party speaking; 1 = one of the two, or the elevator only implied; 0 = neither, or the line is not small talk.

criteria.brief: Sounds like a machine talking, with robot logic, sensors, firmware or charging habits showing through the politeness.
criteria.grading: 2 = a machine fact is doing the work of the sentence (firmware, version, an instruction the machine obeys); 1 = a machine word sits in it without carrying the line; 0 = nothing machine about it.

criteria.brief: Lands the awkwardness: the pause, the forced courtesy, the thing neither robot wants to name.
criteria.grading: 2 = a pause or a hedge, and something left deliberately unnamed; 1 = courtesy with nothing under it; 0 = neither.

criteria.brief: Is funny on the first read, with a turn that surprises rather than a pun everyone has heard before.
criteria.grading: 2 = the last words reframe the line and it still lands at once; 1 = a small reversal, or a shape already well worn; 0 = no turn, or the joke needs a second read.

criteria.brief: Stays tight as a single line, with every word earning its place and no setup wasted.
criteria.grading: 2 = under 90 characters and no clause that could go; 1 = a second clause that only decorates; 0 = setup wasted or the line runs past 150 characters.

tie_break: On equal score: fewer bytes, then lexicographic order. The contest itself settles an exact tie by the smaller text before the earlier receipt, so the same order is used here.

candidates.note: The elevator act and nothing else: no machine in it, no courtesy, no turn.

candidates.line: Nice weather for a ride, isn't it?
candidates.note: Two robots, an elevator implied by 'ride', the forced courtesy of 'isn't it' — and the joke everyone has heard.

candidates.line: Hello, fellow robot. Do you come here often?
candidates.note: A bar line wearing a robot's hello, and 'here' is nowhere in particular.

candidates.line: Going up? I'd offer small talk, but they uninstalled it to make room for the new navigation firmware.
candidates.note: Machine logic doing real work, but 'they uninstalled' hands the sentence to an absent installer and the clause is long.

candidates.line: Going up? I only ask because I'm not allowed to make small talk since the incident.
candidates.note: 'Not allowed' is a machine obeying a rule and 'the incident' is exactly the thing neither wants to name. The machine shows only as bureaucracy, never as a part.

candidates.line: Going up? I'm contractually obliged to ask about your firmware version.
candidates.note: Firmware version is the machine talking through courtesy; the obligation is decor rather than a machine fact, and the shape is a familiar one.

candidates.line: Going up? I'm on 4.2. Sorry — is that not the small talk?
candidates.note: The tightest of the strong ones and the courtesy lands, but '4.2' is a version dropped in rather than a machine fact carrying the sentence, and the turn is only self-aware.

candidates.line: Which floor? Also, my small talk counts as a firmware event, so keep it short.
candidates.note: A firmware event is a strong machine turn, but 'so keep it short' is a second instruction tacked on and the second robot is only talked at.

candidates.line: Going up? My firmware insists I ask your version. ...Same as mine, isn't it.
candidates.note: Firmware is the speaker: it insists, so the courtesy is a machine's, not a person's. The pause is written, and the last words name what neither wants to name — they are the same unit. It lands at once and wastes no setup.

candidates.line: Going up? Eleven floors of battery left and zero more topics.
candidates.note: Battery is a good machine fact and the count is tight, but nobody is addressed and there is no courtesy at all.

candidates.line: Third floor? Great. We both know neither of us is getting the firmware update.
candidates.note: 'We both know' does the awkward sharing well, but three sentences of setup for one turn.

candidates.line: You're the replacement unit. Of course you are. ...So, which floor?
candidates.note: The pause and the thing neither names are both there, but the machine shows only as vocabulary and the turn is the recognition itself, not its last words.
